candidates.topic: The Man Who Never Forgot a Single Day — AJ
candidates.teaser: She can replay any day of her life like a video — but it's not a superpower, it's a curse.
candidates.video_title: She Remembers Every Second of Her Life
candidates.video_description: Jill Price, known as AJ in scientific literature, was the first person diagnosed with hyperthymesia — the inability to forget any day of her life. While it sounds like a gift, she described it as an uncontrollable, exhausting mental prison.
candidates.script: She can tell you exactly what she ate for breakfast on March 14th, 1988 — without trying. Jill Price was the first human ever diagnosed with perfect autobiographical memory. Every single day since she was 14 plays on a constant loop inside her mind. Scientists called it hyperthymesia. She called it a burden. While you forget most of your life, she cannot forget a single second of hers. Would you want that ability — or would it slowly destroy you?

candidates.topic: The Candle That Burns Under Water — Thermite
candidates.teaser: There's a substance on Earth that keeps burning even when you drown it — water makes it worse.
candidates.video_title: This Fire Cannot Be Put Out With Water
candidates.video_description: Thermite burns at over 2,500 degrees Celsius and produces its own oxygen during the reaction, meaning water doesn't extinguish it — it can actually accelerate the explosion. Used in military incendiary devices and industrial welding, it is one of the most unstoppable chemical reactions known.
candidates.script: Pour water on this fire and it explodes. Thermite burns at 2,500 degrees Celsius — hotter than the surface of some stars — and generates its own oxygen as it burns. That means no water, no sand, nothing can stop it once it starts. It melts through steel in seconds. Militaries have used it in incendiary bombs. Welders use it to fuse railway tracks. The reaction lasts only seconds, but the destruction it leaves behind is permanent. What would you even do against something like this?

candidates.topic: The Island Owned by a Single Family for 900 Years — Sark
candidates.teaser: There's a tiny island in Europe where cars are banned, there's no income tax — and one family ruled it for nearly a thousand years.
candidates.video_title: The Island That Refused the Modern World
candidates.video_description: Sark, a tiny island in the English Channel, was a feudal state until 2008 — the last feudal territory in the Western world. For nearly 450 years it was ruled by a single hereditary lord, cars were banned, and there was no income tax. Its transition to democracy was forced by a legal battle from two billionaire brothers.
candidates.script: Until 2008, one island in Europe had no democracy, no cars, no income tax — and a single lord who controlled everything. Sark, a three-mile island in the English Channel, was the last feudal state in the Western world. Its ruler inherited absolute power through a system unchanged since 1565. It took two billionaire brothers filing a human rights lawsuit to finally force elections. A place frozen in medieval law survived into the age of smartphones. How did no one notice sooner?

candidates.topic: The Color That Didn't Exist Until 1850 — Blue
candidates.teaser: Ancient civilizations couldn't see the color blue — not because they were blind, but because it didn't exist in their world.
candidates.video_title: Ancient Humans Literally Could Not See Blue
candidates.video_description: Linguists and cognitive scientists discovered that ancient languages, including Homer's Greek, had no word for blue. The Himba tribe of Namibia, who still lack a word for it today, genuinely struggle to distinguish blue from green in tests. If your language has no word for a color, your brain may not register it as distinct.
candidates.script: Homer described the ocean as "wine-dark" — because ancient Greeks had no word for blue. And scientists now believe if you have no word for a color, your brain genuinely cannot isolate it. The Himba tribe in Namibia still have no word for blue today, and in lab tests they cannot separate a blue square from a field of green ones. Blue pigment barely existed in nature. The sky was just... nothing. When did blue become real to you?

candidates.topic: The Neutron Star So Dense a Teaspoon Weighs a Billion Tons
candidates.teaser: There's an object in space so impossibly dense that a single spoonful of it would sink straight through the Earth.
candidates.video_title: One Spoonful of This Would Destroy Earth
candidates.video_description: Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of massive stars, compressed to a diameter of roughly 20 kilometers but containing more mass than our Sun. A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh approximately one billion tons on Earth. They also spin hundreds of times per second, emitting beams of radiation detectable across the galaxy.
candidates.script: A dead star the size of a city is somehow heavier than our entire Sun. Neutron stars collapse so violently that a single teaspoon of their core weighs one billion tons. Drop it on Earth and it falls straight through to the other side. Some of them spin 700 times per second, firing radiation beams across the galaxy like a cosmic lighthouse. They are the most extreme objects in existence that haven't yet crossed into a black hole. What exactly is the line between a star and nothing?
